claim: The Lon AAA+ protease (LonA) is a ubiquitous ATP-dependent proteolytic machine.
source: The Lon AAA+ protease (LonA) is a ubiquitous ATP-dependent proteolytic machine, which selectively degrades damaged proteins or native proteins carrying exposed motifs (degrons).
evidence: This is a general characterization of LonA supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: LonA selectively degrades damaged proteins or native proteins carrying exposed motifs (degrons).
source: The Lon AAA+ protease (LonA) is a ubiquitous ATP-dependent proteolytic machine, which selectively degrades damaged proteins or native proteins carrying exposed motifs (degrons).
evidence: This is a well-established function of LonA supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: The six NTDs are attached to the hexameric LonA chamber by flexible linkers.
source: The results reveal that the six NTDs are attached to the hexameric LonA chamber by flexible linkers such that the formers tumble independently of the latter.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR spectroscopy data presented in the manuscript showing independent tumbling of NTDs.

claim: The NTDs tumble independently of the hexameric LonA chamber.
source: The results reveal that the six NTDs are attached to the hexameric LonA chamber by flexible linkers such that the formers tumble independently of the latter.
evidence: This is demonstrated by NMR spectroscopy experiments comparing isolated NTD and full-length LonA.

claim: The NTD selectively interacts with unfolded proteins by two hydrophobic patches of its N-lobe.
source: Further spectral analyses show that the NTD selectively interacts with unfolded proteins, protein aggregates, and degron-tagged proteins by two hydrophobic patches of its N-lobe, but not intrinsically disordered substrate, α-casein.
evidence: This is supported by NMR chemical shift perturbation mapping and mutagenesis studies.

claim: The NTD selectively interacts with protein aggregates by two hydrophobic patches of its N-lobe.
source: Further spectral analyses show that the NTD selectively interacts with unfolded proteins, protein aggregates, and degron-tagged proteins by two hydrophobic patches of its N-lobe, but not intrinsically disordered substrate, α-casein.
evidence: This is supported by NMR experiments with TCEP-treated denatured lysozyme.

claim: The NTD selectively interacts with degron-tagged proteins by two hydrophobic patches of its N-lobe.
source: Further spectral analyses show that the NTD selectively interacts with unfolded proteins, protein aggregates, and degron-tagged proteins by two hydrophobic patches of its N-lobe, but not intrinsically disordered substrate, α-casein.
evidence: This is supported by NMR titration experiments with Sul20 peptide and degron-tagged proteins.

claim: The NTD does not interact with intrinsically disordered substrate α-casein.
source: Further spectral analyses show that the NTD selectively interacts with unfolded proteins, protein aggregates, and degron-tagged proteins by two hydrophobic patches of its N-lobe, but not intrinsically disordered substrate, α-casein.
evidence: This is demonstrated by NMR experiments showing no significant chemical shift perturbations upon addition of α-casein.

claim: The NTD selectively binds to protein substrates when they are thermally induced to adopt unfolded conformations.
source: Moreover, the NTD selectively binds to protein substrates when they are thermally induced to adopt unfolded conformations.
evidence: This is demonstrated by temperature cycling NMR experiments with Ig2 and Ig2D5.

claim: NTDs enable LonA to perform protein quality control to selectively degrade proteins in damaged states.
source: Collectively, our findings demonstrate that NTDs enable LonA to perform protein quality control to selectively degrade proteins in damaged states and suggest that substrate discrimination and selective degradation by LonA are mediated by multiple NTD interactions.
evidence: This is supported by degradation assays and NMR binding studies.

claim: Substrate discrimination and selective degradation by LonA are mediated by multiple NTD interactions.
source: Collectively, our findings demonstrate that NTDs enable LonA to perform protein quality control to selectively degrade proteins in damaged states and suggest that substrate discrimination and selective degradation by LonA are mediated by multiple NTD interactions.
evidence: This is suggested based on NMR data showing multiple NTDs can interact with substrates.

claim: LonA was previously known as protease La.
source: The Lon AAA+ protease (LonA), previously known as the protease La, is an ATP-dependent protease distributed in prokaryotes and eukaryotes (Charette et al., 1981).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to historical literature.

claim: LonA is an ATP-dependent protease distributed in prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
source: The Lon AAA+ protease (LonA), previously known as the protease La, is an ATP-dependent protease distributed in prokaryotes and eukaryotes (Charette et al., 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Charette et al., 1981.

claim: LonA forms a homo-hexamer to execute its biological function.
source: It forms a homo-hexamer to execute its biological function (Park et al., 2006; Goldberg et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Park et al., 2006 and Goldberg et al., 1994.

claim: LonA belongs to the AAA+ (ATPases associated with various cellular activities) superfamily.
source: LonA belongs to the AAA+ (ATPases associated with various cellular activities) superfamily and contains an N-terminal domain (NTD), a middle ATPase domain with conserved Walker motifs for ATP hydrolysis, and a C-terminal protease domain (CTD) with a serine-lysine catalytic dyad in the active site (Rotanova et al., 2004; Botos et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rotanova et al., 2004 and Botos et al., 2004.

claim: LonA contains an N-terminal domain (NTD), a middle ATPase domain with conserved Walker motifs for ATP hydrolysis, and a C-terminal protease domain (CTD) with a serine-lysine catalytic dyad in the active site.
source: LonA belongs to the AAA+ (ATPases associated with various cellular activities) superfamily and contains an N-terminal domain (NTD), a middle ATPase domain with conserved Walker motifs for ATP hydrolysis, and a C-terminal protease domain (CTD) with a serine-lysine catalytic dyad in the active site (Rotanova et al., 2004; Botos et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rotanova et al., 2004 and Botos et al., 2004.

claim: LonA is responsible for degrading damaged or unfolded proteins, as well as native proteins bearing specific recognition elements, known as degradation tags or degrons.
source: LonA is responsible for degrading damaged or unfolded proteins, as well as native proteins bearing specific recognition elements, known as degradation tags or degrons (Higashitani et al., 1997; Wohlever et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Higashitani et al., 1997 and Wohlever et al., 2014.

claim: Substrate recognition of LonA is thought to be mediated by its NTD.
source: Substrate recognition of LonA is thought to be mediated by its NTD (Ebel et al., 1999; Roudiak and Shrader, 1998; Rudyak and Shrader, 2000; Iyer et al., 2004; Melnikov et al., 2008; Adam et al., 2012; Cheng et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The substrates are unfolded and translocated in an ATP-dependent process into a secluded chamber formed by the ATPase and protease domains.
source: The substrates are unfolded and translocated in an ATP-dependent process into a secluded chamber formed by the ATPase and protease domains.
evidence: This is established knowledge about LonA mechanism.

claim: The unfolded substrates inside the chamber can be degraded into small peptide fragments.
source: Finally, the unfolded substrates inside the chamber can be degraded into small peptide fragments (Gottesman, 2003; Baker and Sauer, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gottesman, 2003 and Baker and Sauer, 2006.

claim: The ATP-dependent translocation process of substrates into the hexameric chamber has been well characterized.
source: The ATP-dependent translocation process of substrates into the hexameric chamber has been well characterized (Lin et al., 2016; Su et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lin et al., 2016 and Su et al., 2016.

claim: Structures of different N-terminal fragments of LonA had been reported, including Escherichia coli (EcLon), Mycobacterium avium complex (MacLon), and Bacillus subtilis (BsLon).
source: Structures of different N-terminal fragments of LonA had been reported (Li et al., 2005; Duman and Löwe, 2010; Li et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2019), including Escherichia coli (EcLon), Mycobacterium avium complex (MacLon), and Bacillus subtilis (BsLon).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple structural studies.

claim: No structural study has been conducted to analyze substrate interactions by the NTD either in isolation or in the context of full-length LonA.
source: However, no structural study has been conducted to analyze substrate interactions by the NTD either in isolation or in the context of full-length LonA.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in existing literature that this study addresses.

claim: MtaLonA is a thermal stable LonA isolated from Meiothermus taiwanensis.
source: To understand how LonA selectively recognizes protein substrates being in damaged states, we have used a thermal stable LonA isolated from Meiothermus taiwanensis (termed MtaLonA henceforth), which allows temperature cycling experiments to be used for switching the populations of protein substrates in the folded and unfolded states.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental system used in the study.

claim: MtaLonA allows temperature cycling experiments to be used for switching the populations of protein substrates in the folded and unfolded states.
source: To understand how LonA selectively recognizes protein substrates being in damaged states, we have used a thermal stable LonA isolated from Meiothermus taiwanensis (termed MtaLonA henceforth), which allows temperature cycling experiments to be used for switching the populations of protein substrates in the folded and unfolded states.
evidence: This is supported by the thermal stability data and experimental design.

claim: Ig2 is a dimer with an immunoglobulin (Ig) fold that is natively folded up to 40°C.
source: In this work, five various protein substrates have been employed for NMR experiments, which include (1) Ig2 (domains 5 and 6 of the gelation factor from Dictyostelium discoideum [Hsu et al., 2009], hereafter abbreviated as Ig2) with an immunoglobulin (Ig) fold forming a dimer that is natively folded up to 40°C
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hsu et al., 2009 and thermal stability measurements.

claim: α-casein is an intrinsically disordered protein with no tertiary structure.
source: (2) α-casein, which is an intrinsically disordered protein with no tertiary structure
evidence: This is established knowledge about α-casein.

claim: Native lysozyme has four disulfide bridges.
source: (3) native lysozyme with four disulfide bridges and reduced lysozyme forming loose and flexible aggregates
evidence: This is established knowledge about lysozyme structure.

claim: Reduced lysozyme forms loose and flexible aggregates.
source: (3) native lysozyme with four disulfide bridges and reduced lysozyme forming loose and flexible aggregates
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2015 in the manuscript.

claim: The presence of MtaLonA NTD is required to degrade damaged proteins.
source: Our results show that the presence of MtaLonA NTD is required to degrade damaged proteins and native proteins with degrons, but it does not play an active role in mediating the degradation by LonA of an intrinsically disordered substrate, α-casein.
evidence: This is supported by degradation assays comparing full-length MtaLonA and AAAP.

claim: The presence of MtaLonA NTD is required to degrade native proteins with degrons.
source: Our results show that the presence of MtaLonA NTD is required to degrade damaged proteins and native proteins with degrons, but it does not play an active role in mediating the degradation by LonA of an intrinsically disordered substrate, α-casein.
evidence: This is supported by degradation assays with degron-tagged substrates.

claim: MtaLonA NTD does not play an active role in mediating the degradation by LonA of an intrinsically disordered substrate, α-casein.
source: Our results show that the presence of MtaLonA NTD is required to degrade damaged proteins and native proteins with degrons, but it does not play an active role in mediating the degradation by LonA of an intrinsically disordered substrate, α-casein.
evidence: This is supported by degradation assays and NMR experiments showing no interaction between NTD and α-casein.

claim: The crystal structure of an N-terminal fragment of MtaLonA was determined at a 2.1 Å resolution.
source: Here we report the crystal structure of an N-terminal fragment of MtaLonA determined at a 2.1 Å resolution, demonstrating that it is similar to the structures of both EcLon and MacLon NTDs, but not to that of BsLon.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data presented in Table 1.

claim: The structure of MtaLonA NTD is similar to the structures of both EcLon and MacLon NTDs, but not to that of BsLon.
source: Here we report the crystal structure of an N-terminal fragment of MtaLonA determined at a 2.1 Å resolution, demonstrating that it is similar to the structures of both EcLon and MacLon NTDs, but not to that of BsLon.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison and alignment data.

claim: MtaLonA NTD appears to tumble independently of the hexameric core complex.
source: MtaLonA NTD appears to tumble independently of the hexameric core complex, indicating that the NTD is attached to the hexameric chamber by a flexible linker thus rendering it possible for detailed chemical shift perturbation (CSP) mapping of substrate binding in the context of full-length MtaLonA.
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectroscopy data comparing isolated NTD and full-length LonA.

claim: The NTD is attached to the hexameric chamber by a flexible linker.
source: MtaLonA NTD appears to tumble independently of the hexameric core complex, indicating that the NTD is attached to the hexameric chamber by a flexible linker thus rendering it possible for detailed chemical shift perturbation (CSP) mapping of substrate binding in the context of full-length MtaLonA.
evidence: This is inferred from the independent tumbling observed by NMR and supported by crystallographic data.

claim: The flexible linker allows detailed chemical shift perturbation (CSP) mapping of substrate binding in the context of full-length MtaLonA.
source: MtaLonA NTD appears to tumble independently of the hexameric core complex, indicating that the NTD is attached to the hexameric chamber by a flexible linker thus rendering it possible for detailed chemical shift perturbation (CSP) mapping of substrate binding in the context of full-length MtaLonA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the favorable NMR properties observed.

claim: The flexibly linked NTDs can help survey, discriminate, and selectively capture damaged unfolded protein species or native protein substrates carrying exposed degradation sequence motifs.
source: This work suggests that the flexibly linked NTDs can help survey, discriminate, and selectively capture damaged unfolded protein species or native protein substrates carrying exposed degradation sequence motifs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural and binding data presented in the study.

claim: AAAP exhibited a slightly reduced degradation activity against α-casein compared to full-length MtaLonA.
source: Compared to the full-length MtaLonA, AAAP exhibited a slightly reduced degradation activity against α-casein (Figure 1B), while its proteolytic activity for thermally unfolded Ig2 was severely impaired (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by degradation assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: AAAP's proteolytic activity for thermally unfolded Ig2 was severely impaired compared to full-length MtaLonA.
source: Compared to the full-length MtaLonA, AAAP exhibited a slightly reduced degradation activity against α-casein (Figure 1B), while its proteolytic activity for thermally unfolded Ig2 was severely impaired (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by degradation assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Despite the lack of the NTD, AAAP retains the proteolytic activity for intrinsically disordered protein substrates like α-casein.
source: These results showed that, despite the lack of the NTD, AAAP retains the proteolytic activity for intrinsically disordered protein substrates like α-casein.
evidence: This is supported by the degradation assay data.

claim: The NTD is essential for MtaLonA to recognize and degrade the thermally damaged substrate, Ig2.
source: However, the NTD is essential for MtaLonA to recognize and degrade the thermally damaged substrate, Ig2, indicating the NTD may mediate specific interactions with damaged Ig2, but not α-casein.
evidence: This is supported by the degradation assay comparing full-length and AAAP.

claim: The NTD may mediate specific interactions with damaged Ig2, but not α-casein.
source: However, the NTD is essential for MtaLonA to recognize and degrade the thermally damaged substrate, Ig2, indicating the NTD may mediate specific interactions with damaged Ig2, but not α-casein.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential degradation activities and NMR binding studies.

claim: The melting temperature of MtaLonA is 68°C.
source: The melting temperatures of MtaLonA and NN206 are 68°C and 85.5°C, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by thermal shift assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The melting temperature of NN206 is 85.5°C.
source: The melting temperatures of MtaLonA and NN206 are 68°C and 85.5°C, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by thermal shift assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Tm of substrate Ig2 is 46°C.
source: The Tm of substrate Ig2 is 46°C, suggesting that the structure of Ig2 is thermal denatured as a substrate of MtaLonA at 55°C.
evidence: This is supported by thermal shift assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The structure of Ig2 is thermally denatured as a substrate of MtaLonA at 55°C.
source: The Tm of substrate Ig2 is 46°C, suggesting that the structure of Ig2 is thermal denatured as a substrate of MtaLonA at 55°C.
evidence: This is inferred from the Tm being lower than the experimental temperature.

claim: NN206 forms a bilobal fold consisting of an N-terminal lobe and a C-terminal lobe.
source: NN206 forms a bilobal fold: (1) the N-terminal lobe, which consists of one α-helix and six β-strands, forming three β-sheets (β1/β3/β4/β5, β2/β5/β4, and β1/β6/β5); (2) the C-terminal lobe, which is exclusively α-helical, consisting of a five-helix bundle (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The N-terminal lobe of NN206 consists of one α-helix and six β-strands, forming three β-sheets.
source: NN206 forms a bilobal fold: (1) the N-terminal lobe, which consists of one α-helix and six β-strands, forming three β-sheets (β1/β3/β4/β5, β2/β5/β4, and β1/β6/β5); (2) the C-terminal lobe, which is exclusively α-helical, consisting of a five-helix bundle (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The C-terminal lobe of NN206 is exclusively α-helical, consisting of a five-helix bundle.
source: NN206 forms a bilobal fold: (1) the N-terminal lobe, which consists of one α-helix and six β-strands, forming three β-sheets (β1/β3/β4/β5, β2/β5/β4, and β1/β6/β5); (2) the C-terminal lobe, which is exclusively α-helical, consisting of a five-helix bundle (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The two lobes of NN206 are jointed together by an 18-residue linker.
source: The two lobes are jointed together by an 18-residue linker, which is similar to that of both EcLon and MacLon (Li et al., 2005; Duman and Löwe, 2010; Li et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure and comparison with other LonA NTD structures.

claim: The structure of NN291 is very similar to that of NN206 except for a longer C-terminal helix by four more residues.
source: The structure of NN291, refined to 1.7 Å resolution (Table 1), is very similar to that of NN206 except for a longer C-terminal helix by four more residues, that is, residues 207–210 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure comparison shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No electron density was seen past residue A210 in the NN291 structure.
source: Despite the lack of spontaneous proteolytic fragmentation in the crystals, no electron density was seen past residue A210 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the electron density map shown in Figure 2D.

claim: About 200 well-resolved correlations of NN206 and full-length MtaLonA are superimposable in NMR spectra.
source: With the aid of perdeuteration labeling and transverse relaxation optimized spectroscopy (TROSY), we observed over 200 well-resolved 15N-1H correlations of full-length hexameric MtaLonA at an apparent molecular weight of 0.5 MDa. Importantly, most of these correlations were very similar to those observed in the NN206 spectrum (Figure 2E) and a systematic chemical shift offset was due to deuterium isotope effects.
evidence: This is supported by the NMR spectra comparison shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The NTD adopts the same structure as the isolated NTD while loosely tethered to the near-megadalton hexameric LonA core via a long flexible linker.
source: These results indicated that the NTD adopts the same structure as the isolated NTD while loosely tethered to the near-megadalton hexameric LonA core via a long flexible linker leading to an independently fast tumbling motion to yield highly favorable NMR relaxation properties and thus high-quality multidimensional NMR spectra (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR spectral similarity and favorable relaxation properties.

claim: The NMR-derived secondary structure of NN206 is highly similar to its solved X-ray structures.
source: We further applied multidimensional heteronuclear NMR experiments to assign the observed cross-peaks in 1H–15N TROSY-HSQC spectrum of NN206 (BMRB code: 50697) and the NMR-derived secondary structure of NN206, based on the Chemical Shift Index (Hafsa et al., 2015), was highly similar to its solved X-ray structures (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of NMR-derived and X-ray structures shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Each of the six NTDs may connect to the hexameric core by a flexible ~40-residue linker.
source: Together, these results suggested that in a MtaLonA complex, each of the six NTDs may connect to the hexameric core by a flexible ~40-residue linker.
evidence: This is inferred from crystallographic and NMR data showing disorder in this region.

claim: Each 24-kDa NTD may tumble independently of the 350-kDa hexameric core.
source: Therefore, each 24-kDa NTD may tumble independently of the 350-kDa hexameric core (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR data showing favorable relaxation properties.

claim: Thermal cycling of isolated NN206 exhibited no temperature effects on its protein structure.
source: By contrast, thermal cycling of isolated NN206 exhibited no temperature effects on its protein structure monitored by NMR spectroscopy (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), which could be explained by the high melting temperatures (Tm) of full-length MtaLonA and NN206 (68.0°C and 85.5°C, respectively; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectra before and after thermal cycling shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Upon addition of well-folded Ig2 at 32°C, no significant CSPs were observed for NN206.
source: Upon addition of a twofold molar excess of well-folded Ig2 at 32°C, no significant CSPs were observed (Figure 3A), where only the NN206 was isotopically enriched.
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectra shown in Figure 3A.

claim: By increasing temperature from 32°C to 55°C, dramatic variations in the 2D spectral features were detected and the resonances underwent a prominent decrease in intensity for NN206 in the presence of Ig2.
source: By increasing temperature from 32°C to 55°C for the same NMR sample, dramatic variations in the 2D spectral features were detected and the resonances underwent a prominent decrease in intensity (Figure 3B), indicating that the NTD interacts with thermally unfolded Ig2.
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectra shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The NTD interacts with thermally unfolded Ig2.
source: By increasing temperature from 32°C to 55°C for the same NMR sample, dramatic variations in the 2D spectral features were detected and the resonances underwent a prominent decrease in intensity (Figure 3B), indicating that the NTD interacts with thermally unfolded Ig2.
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR spectral changes upon heating.

claim: With temperature dropping from 55°C to 32°C, linewidth of the expected bound-state resonances was too broad to be detected in the presence of binding events.
source: With temperature dropping from 55°C to 32°C, linewidth of the expected bound-state resonances was too broad to be detected in the presence of binding events (Figure 3C), suggesting a certain portion of Ig2 still stays in the unfolded or aggregated state.
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectra shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A certain portion of Ig2 still stays in the unfolded or aggregated state after cooling from 55°C to 32°C.
source: With temperature dropping from 55°C to 32°C, linewidth of the expected bound-state resonances was too broad to be detected in the presence of binding events (Figure 3C), suggesting a certain portion of Ig2 still stays in the unfolded or aggregated state.
evidence: This is inferred from the broad linewidths and SEC data.

claim: The addition of α-casein resulted in little to no effect on the cross-peaks of residues 1–206 of the NTD.
source: In contrast, the addition of α-casein resulted in little to no effect on the cross-peaks of residues 1–206 of the NTD (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B), thus precluding specific interaction mode between the intrinsically disordered protein α-casein and MtaLonA NTD.
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectra shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: There is no specific interaction mode between the intrinsically disordered protein α-casein and MtaLonA NTD.
source: In contrast, the addition of α-casein resulted in little to no effect on the cross-peaks of residues 1–206 of the NTD (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B), thus precluding specific interaction mode between the intrinsically disordered protein α-casein and MtaLonA NTD.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of NMR spectral changes.

claim: More than half of Ig2 protein became unfolded or aggregated through one thermal cycle.
source: The analysis revealed that more than half of Ig2 protein became unfolded or aggregated through one thermal cycle while the NTD was still well-folded (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The NTD was still well-folded after one thermal cycle with Ig2.
source: The analysis revealed that more than half of Ig2 protein became unfolded or aggregated through one thermal cycle while the NTD was still well-folded (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The NTD-Ig2 aggregate complex showed a dissociable SEC profile.
source: The NTD-Ig2 aggregate complex showed a dissociable SEC profile, suggesting the NTD-substrate interaction is quite dynamic by nature and the fast substrate dissociation may facilitate the translocation process.
evidence: This is supported by SEC data and inferred to have functional implications.

claim: The NTD-substrate interaction is quite dynamic by nature.
source: The NTD-Ig2 aggregate complex showed a dissociable SEC profile, suggesting the NTD-substrate interaction is quite dynamic by nature and the fast substrate dissociation may facilitate the translocation process.
evidence: This is inferred from the dissociable SEC profile.

claim: The fast substrate dissociation may facilitate the translocation process.
source: The NTD-Ig2 aggregate complex showed a dissociable SEC profile, suggesting the NTD-substrate interaction is quite dynamic by nature and the fast substrate dissociation may facilitate the translocation process.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed dynamic interaction.

claim: Thermally damaged Ig2 induces significant CSPs and broadened resonances in the NTD N-lobe.
source: NMR analysis indicates that thermally damaged Ig2 induces significant CSPs and broadened resonances in the NTD N-lobe, which comprises one α-helix and three β-sheets β1/β3/β4/β5, β2/β5/β4 and β1/β6/β5.
evidence: This is supported by NMR CSP mapping data.

claim: The residues of MtaLonA NTD with the pronounced CSPs are part of the interaction interface located mainly at helix α1, loop L1, L2, L3, and β-sheet β2/β5/β4.
source: The residues of MtaLonA NTD with the pronounced CSPs are part of the interaction interface located mainly at helix α1, loop L1, L2, L3, and β-sheet β2/β5/β4 (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4A), which consist primarily of hydrophobic residues and are decorated by a number of polar residues (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by NMR CSP mapping shown in Figure 3E and supplementary figures.

claim: The interaction interface consists primarily of hydrophobic residues and are decorated by a number of polar residues.
source: The residues of MtaLonA NTD with the pronounced CSPs are part of the interaction interface located mainly at helix α1, loop L1, L2, L3, and β-sheet β2/β5/β4 (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4A), which consist primarily of hydrophobic residues and are decorated by a number of polar residues (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of the binding interface.

claim: NN206* containing two specific mutations P22A and M85A showed much weak interactions with thermal damaged Ig2.
source: NN206* showed much weak interactions with thermal damaged Ig2 (Figure 3F–H and Figure 3—figure supplement 4F), confirming that this binding event is mainly contributed by the specific hydrophobic residues with high hydrophobicity in the N-lobe.
evidence: This is supported by NMR titration data shown in Figure 3F–H.

claim: The binding event between NTD and damaged Ig2 is mainly contributed by the specific hydrophobic residues with high hydrophobicity in the N-lobe.
source: NN206* showed much weak interactions with thermal damaged Ig2 (Figure 3F–H and Figure 3—figure supplement 4F), confirming that this binding event is mainly contributed by the specific hydrophobic residues with high hydrophobicity in the N-lobe.
evidence: This is confirmed by mutagenesis studies.

claim: The NTD of LonA selectively interacts with protein substrates via critical hydrophobic residues of its N-lobe.
source: Collectively, our results showed that the NTD of LonA selectively interacts with protein substrates via critical hydrophobic residues of its N-lobe, demonstrating that the NTD enables LonA to perform protein quality control by selectively interacting with proteins in damaged or unfolded states.
evidence: This is supported by NMR binding studies and mutagenesis.

claim: Native lysozyme is a 14.3-kDa protein comprising four disulfide bridges.
source: Native lysozyme is a 14.3-kDa protein (129 amino acids) comprising four disulfide bridges while reduced lysozyme forms loose and flexible aggregates (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about lysozyme supported by citation.

claim: TCEP drives the formation of amorphous lysozyme aggregates.
source: TCEP (Tris (2-carboxyethyl) phosphine; nonthiol-based reducing agent) drives the formation of amorphous lysozyme aggregates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TCEP's effect on lysozyme.

claim: There is no cysteine residue found in full-length MtaLonA.
source: Moreover, there is no cysteine residue found in full-length MtaLonA, suggesting TCEP does not affect the structure of MtaLonA NTD.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: TCEP does not affect the structure of MtaLonA NTD.
source: Moreover, there is no cysteine residue found in full-length MtaLonA, suggesting TCEP does not affect the structure of MtaLonA NTD.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of cysteine residues.

claim: Addition of TCEP-treated denatured lysozyme led to substantial spectral changes of NN206 resonances recorded at 32°C.
source: Addition of TCEP-treated denatured lysozyme leaded to substantial spectral changes of NN206 resonances recorded at 32°C, while NN206* only showed marginal CSPs (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectra shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A.

claim: NN206* only showed marginal CSPs upon addition of TCEP-treated denatured lysozyme.
source: Addition of TCEP-treated denatured lysozyme leaded to substantial spectral changes of NN206 resonances recorded at 32°C, while NN206* only showed marginal CSPs (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectra shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A.

claim: The affected residues upon binding denatured lysozyme were located mainly in the N-lobe.
source: The structural mapping showed that the affected residues were also located mainly in the N-lobe shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5B and C.
evidence: This is supported by structural mapping shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5B and C.

claim: Full-length MtaLonA can efficiently degrade denatured-reduced lysozyme, but not native lysozyme.
source: A gel-based assay showed that full-length MtaLonA can efficiently degrade denatured-reduced lysozyme, but not native lysozyme (Figure 3—figure supplement 5D).
evidence: This is supported by degradation assay shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5D.

claim: AAAP, without the NTD, was inactive against either the scrambled lysozyme aggregate or native lysozyme.
source: Accordingly, AAAP, without the NTD, was inactive against either the scrambled lysozyme aggregate or native lysozyme (Figure 3—figure supplement 5E).
evidence: This is supported by degradation assay shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5E.

claim: The NTD plays a key role in discriminating and recognizing protein aggregates before subsequent translocation and degradation.
source: Together, these results highlighted the key role of NTD, via the N-lobe region, in discriminating and recognizing protein aggregates before subsequent translocation and degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from the degradation and binding studies with lysozyme aggregates.

claim: The NTD of E. coli LonA was shown to be required for degron binding by chemical cross-linking.
source: Previously, the NTD of E. coli LonA was shown to be required for degron binding by chemical cross-linking (Wohlever et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wohlever et al., 2014.

claim: Addition of unlabeled Sul20 caused significant spectral changes of NN206 resonances.
source: Addition of unlabeled Sul20 caused significant spectral changes of NN206 resonances (Figure 4A) and the structural mapping showed that the affected residues were again located at β‐sheet β2/β5/β4, loop L1, L3, and helix α1 of the N-lobe subdomain (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectra shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The affected residues upon Sul20 binding were located at β‐sheet β2/β5/β4, loop L1, L3, and helix α1 of the N-lobe subdomain.
source: Addition of unlabeled Sul20 caused significant spectral changes of NN206 resonances (Figure 4A) and the structural mapping showed that the affected residues were again located at β‐sheet β2/β5/β4, loop L1, L3, and helix α1 of the N-lobe subdomain (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by structural mapping shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mutations of P22 and M85 to Alanine led to much weak binding of NN206* with Sul20 peptide.
source: Mutations of P22 and M85 located at the center of the hydrophobic surface to moderately hydrophobic Alanine leaded to much weak binding of NN206* with Sul20 peptide (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C), suggesting that specific hydrophobic residues of beta-stranded β2/β5/β4 located at the N-lobe of MtaLon NTD play a critical role in degron recognition.
evidence: This is supported by NMR titration data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Specific hydrophobic residues of beta-stranded β2/β5/β4 located at the N-lobe of MtaLon NTD play a critical role in degron recognition.
source: Mutations of P22 and M85 located at the center of the hydrophobic surface to moderately hydrophobic Alanine leaded to much weak binding of NN206* with Sul20 peptide (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C), suggesting that specific hydrophobic residues of beta-stranded β2/β5/β4 located at the N-lobe of MtaLon NTD play a critical role in degron recognition.
evidence: This is inferred from mutagenesis studies.

claim: The NMR spectra of Ig2D5 and Ig2D5-S20 were well superimposed.
source: The NMR spectra of Ig2D5 and Ig2D5-S20 were well superimposed, indicating that the folded domain structure corresponding to Ig2D5 is not perturbed by the C-terminal Sul20 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectra shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The folded domain structure corresponding to Ig2D5 is not perturbed by the C-terminal Sul20.
source: The NMR spectra of Ig2D5 and Ig2D5-S20 were well superimposed, indicating that the folded domain structure corresponding to Ig2D5 is not perturbed by the C-terminal Sul20 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is inferred from the superimposable NMR spectra.

claim: The NMR-derived secondary structure of Sul20 was flexible random-coil.
source: Furthermore, the NMR spectrum of Ig2D5-S20 exhibited additional cross-peaks that well corresponded to Sul20 and the NMR-derived secondary structure of Sul20 was flexible random-coil (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by NMR chemical shift analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Lower [1H]–15N NOEs for Sul20 residues were due to the increased flexibility on ps-ns timescale.
source: Lower [1H]–15N NOEs for Sul20 residues were due to the increased flexibility on ps-ns timescale.
evidence: This is inferred from NOE measurements.

claim: Residues Y19 and H20 are strongly affected by the binding event based on the resonance broadening beyond detection.
source: By addition of unlabeled NN206 to isotopically enriched Ig2D5-S20, we observed chemical shift changes and broadened resonances of C-terminal Sul20 (Figure 4C and E), suggesting that residues Y19 and H20 are strongly affected by the binding event based on the resonance broadening beyond detection.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4C and E.

claim: The secondary structure of Sul20 remained random coil in the presence of MtaLonA NTD.
source: The secondary structure of Sul20 remained random coil in the presence of MtaLonA NTD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by NMR chemical shift analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Sul20 tag can be recognized by the hydrophobic patches of N-lobe of MtaLon NTD.
source: The NMR spectrum of Ig2D5-S20 in the presence of an equimolar amount of unlabeled NN206* showed a much less pronounced chemical shift effect (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and F) than wild-type NN206 binding to Ig2D5-S20, indicating that Sul20 tag can be recognized by the hydrophobic patches of N-lobe of MtaLon NTD.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of binding with wild-type and mutant NTD.

claim: The degradation by the full-length MtaLonA against Y19A/H20A double mutant of Sul20 was much less efficient.
source: The results showed that the degradation by the full-length MtaLonA against Y19A/H20A double mutant of Sul20 was much less efficient (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by degradation assay shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Y19A/H20A double mutant indeed significantly reduces the binding with NN206.
source: By addition of 15N-labeled NN206 to 15N-labeled Ig2D5-S20-Y19A/H20A, careful comparison of chemical shifts revealed that no obvious changes, suggesting that Y19A/H20A double mutant indeed significantly reduces the binding with NN206 (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: About 96% of the backbone resonances of Ig2D5 can be assigned by multidimensional heteronuclear NMR experiments.
source: About 96% of the backbone resonances of Ig2D5 can be assigned by multidimensional heteronuclear NMR experiments.
evidence: This is based on NMR assignment experiments.

claim: Ig2D5 is a β-sheet protein with Ig-like fold.
source: Ig2D5 is a β-sheet protein with Ig-like fold and the Tm of substrate Ig2D5 is similar to Ig2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is based on NMR and structural analysis.

claim: The Tm of substrate Ig2D5 is similar to Ig2.
source: Ig2D5 is a β-sheet protein with Ig-like fold and the Tm of substrate Ig2D5 is similar to Ig2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by thermal shift assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Isolated Ig2D5 was largely unfolded at 60°C.
source: Based on the intensity changes of resonances corresponding to native Ig2D5, we estimated that isolated Ig2D5 was largely unfolded at 60°C (Figure 5A and B; coloured green) and ~72% of Ig2D5 was folded after one thermal cycle (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on NMR intensity measurements shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: ~72% of Ig2D5 was folded after one thermal cycle in the absence of NN206.
source: Based on the intensity changes of resonances corresponding to native Ig2D5, we estimated that isolated Ig2D5 was largely unfolded at 60°C (Figure 5A and B; coloured green) and ~72% of Ig2D5 was folded after one thermal cycle (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on NMR intensity measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the presence of equimolar NN206, the folded ratio of Ig2D5 was reduced to ~15% after thermal treatment.
source: However, in the presence of equimolar NN206, the folded ratio of Ig2D5 was reduced to ~15% after thermal treatment (Figure 5C; coloured blue).
evidence: This is based on NMR intensity measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Similar results were obtained using equimolar full-length MtaLonA with catalytic mutant S678A (LonA*).
source: Similar results were obtained using equimolar full-length MtaLonA with catalytic mutant S678A (LonA*) (Figure 5C; coloured orange).
evidence: This is based on NMR intensity measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: On addition of equimolar AAAP*, ~75% of Ig2D5 were folded under the same condition.
source: However, on addition of equimolar AAAP* (residues 242–793 with catalytic mutant S678A), ~75% of Ig2D5 were folded under the same condition (Figure 5C; coloured black).
evidence: This is based on NMR intensity measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The unfolded state of Ig2D5 was engaged with MtaLon NTD.
source: The results revealed that the unfolded state of Ig2D5 was engaged with MtaLon NTD and the temperature-induced unfolding-refolding of substrate was significantly affected in the presence of MtaLon NTD (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced folded ratio in the presence of NTD.

claim: The temperature-induced unfolding-refolding of substrate was significantly affected in the presence of MtaLon NTD.
source: The results revealed that the unfolded state of Ig2D5 was engaged with MtaLon NTD and the temperature-induced unfolding-refolding of substrate was significantly affected in the presence of MtaLon NTD (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: After one thermal cycle, about 75% of Ig2D5 was folded in the presence of equimolar NN206*.
source: Accordingly, we also examined how the unfolding-refolding of Ig2D5 could be affected by NN206*. After one thermal cycle, about 75% of Ig2D5 was folded in the presence of equimolar NN206* (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is based on NMR intensity measurements shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Upon addition of eightfold excess of NN206*, about 60% of Ig2D5 was folded.
source: Upon addition of eightfold excess of NN206*, about 60% of Ig2D5 was folded (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that NN206* interacts with denatured protein substrates weakly.
evidence: This is based on NMR intensity measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: NN206* interacts with denatured protein substrates weakly.
source: Upon addition of eightfold excess of NN206*, about 60% of Ig2D5 was folded (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that NN206* interacts with denatured protein substrates weakly.
evidence: This is inferred from the higher folded ratio compared to wild-type NN206.

claim: The conformations of Ig2D5 may be affected by the hydrophobic substrate-binding interaction.
source: These results demonstrated that the conformations of Ig2D5 may be affected by the hydrophobic substrate-binding interaction and the thermally unfolded states of substrate proteins can be stabilized by engagement with the NTDs.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of wild-type and mutant NTD.

claim: The thermally unfolded states of substrate proteins can be stabilized by engagement with the NTDs.
source: These results demonstrated that the conformations of Ig2D5 may be affected by the hydrophobic substrate-binding interaction and the thermally unfolded states of substrate proteins can be stabilized by engagement with the NTDs.
evidence: This is supported by the reduced refolding in the presence of NTD.

claim: By selectively interacting with hydrophobic residues exposed in the thermally unfolded states of substrate proteins, the NTDs prominently perturb temperature-induced unfolding-refolding process of substrates.
source: Thus, by selectively interacting with hydrophobic residues exposed in the thermally unfolded states of substrate proteins, the NTDs prominently perturb temperature-induced unfolding-refolding process of substrates.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the temperature cycling experiments.

claim: The construct AAAP devoid of the NTD retains wild-type ATPase and peptidase activities in LonA.
source: We show that the construct AAAP devoid of the NTD (residues 242–793, ATPase and protease domains), which retains wild-type ATPase and peptidase activities in LonA, lacks the degradation activity against thermally denatured Ig2 while exhibits a wild-type-like activity against α-casein (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by degradation assays shown in Figure 1.

claim: AAAP lacks the degradation activity against thermally denatured Ig2.
source: We show that the construct AAAP devoid of the NTD (residues 242–793, ATPase and protease domains), which retains wild-type ATPase and peptidase activities in LonA, lacks the degradation activity against thermally denatured Ig2 while exhibits a wild-type-like activity against α-casein (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by degradation assays shown in Figure 1.

claim: AAAP exhibits a wild-type-like activity against α-casein.
source: We show that the construct AAAP devoid of the NTD (residues 242–793, ATPase and protease domains), which retains wild-type ATPase and peptidase activities in LonA, lacks the degradation activity against thermally denatured Ig2 while exhibits a wild-type-like activity against α-casein (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by degradation assays shown in Figure 1.

claim: The NTD is specific for denatured or damaged protein substrates, whose hydrophobic core regions normally buried in the folded state become exposed.
source: Therefore, the NTD is specific for denatured or damaged protein substrates, whose hydrophobic core regions normally buried in the folded state become exposed, but not for intrinsically disordered substrates like casein, which contains mainly charged or polar residues and lack hydrophobic regions in the protein sequence.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential degradation and binding activities.

claim: The NTD is not specific for intrinsically disordered substrates like casein, which contains mainly charged or polar residues and lack hydrophobic regions in the protein sequence.
source: Therefore, the NTD is specific for denatured or damaged protein substrates, whose hydrophobic core regions normally buried in the folded state become exposed, but not for intrinsically disordered substrates like casein, which contains mainly charged or polar residues and lack hydrophobic regions in the protein sequence.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of interaction with α-casein.

claim: LonA prefers substrates rich in hydrophobic residues.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that LonA prefers substrates rich in hydrophobic residues (Gur and Sauer, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gur and Sauer, 2008.

claim: The ~40 residue region between the NTD and ATPase–Protease domains is structurally flexible with multiple accessible protease sites.
source: Our crystallographic results of NN206 and NN291 are consistent with previous findings that the ~40 residue region between the NTD and ATPase–Protease domains is structurally flexible with multiple accessible protease sites (Roudiak and Shrader, 1998; Duman and Löwe, 2010; Patterson et al., 2004; Vasilyeva et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data and citations to previous studies.

claim: LonA has two substrate-interacting modes: the NTD-non-requiring mode for intrinsically disordered substrates lacking hydrophobic-rich region, and the NTD-requiring mode for recognizing and trapping damaged/denatured substrates with exposed hydrophobic regions.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that LonA has two substrate-interacting modes: (1) the NTD-non-requiring mode for intrinsically disordered substrates lacking hydrophobic-rich region, which may be engaged directly with the pore-loops in the LonA assembly without involving the six NTDs; (2) the NTD-requiring mode for recognizing and trapping damaged/denatured substrates with exposed hydrophobic regions before their engagement with the pore-loops of the LonA assembly.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data.

claim: The key role of NTD is to enable LonA to perform protein quality control to selectively capture and degrade proteins in damaged unfolded states.
source: The key role of NTD is to enable LonA to perform protein quality control to selectively capture and degrade proteins in damaged unfolded states.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on all the experimental data.

claim: The N-domain of ClpX is required for recognition of adaptors and some substrates.
source: The N-domain of ClpX is required for recognition of adaptors and some substrates (Baker and Sauer, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baker and Sauer, 2012.

claim: The role of ClpB NTD in protein disaggregation is well characterized by NMR spectroscopy.
source: The role of ClpB NTD in protein disaggregation is well characterized by NMR spectroscopy (Rosenzweig et al., 2015), demonstrating that ClpB chaperone recognizes exposed hydrophobic stretches in unfolded or aggregated client proteins via a substrate-binding groove in its NTD.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rosenzweig et al., 2015.

claim: ClpB chaperone recognizes exposed hydrophobic stretches in unfolded or aggregated client proteins via a substrate-binding groove in its NTD.
source: The role of ClpB NTD in protein disaggregation is well characterized by NMR spectroscopy (Rosenzweig et al., 2015), demonstrating that ClpB chaperone recognizes exposed hydrophobic stretches in unfolded or aggregated client proteins via a substrate-binding groove in its NTD.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rosenzweig et al., 2015.

claim: In the presence of ClpB NTD, the stability of client proteins can be seriously affected.
source: In the presence of ClpB NTD, the stability of client proteins can be seriously affected, indicating that the binding of client proteins to ClpB NTD selectively stabilizes their unfolded conformations.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rosenzweig et al., 2015.

claim: The binding of client proteins to ClpB NTD selectively stabilizes their unfolded conformations.
source: In the presence of ClpB NTD, the stability of client proteins can be seriously affected, indicating that the binding of client proteins to ClpB NTD selectively stabilizes their unfolded conformations.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rosenzweig et al., 2015.

claim: Intrinsically disordered α-casein can significantly interact with ClpB NTD, but not MtaLonA NTD.
source: Interestingly, intrinsically disordered α-casein can significantly interact with ClpB NTD, but not MtaLonA NTD.
evidence: This is based on comparison with published data on ClpB and the current study's data on MtaLonA.

claim: The α-helical NTD of ClpB chaperones and the beta-stranded N-lobe of MtaLonA NTD comprise substrate-binding sites that play similar roles in specifically recognizing exposed hydrophobic stretches in unfolded or aggregated proteins.
source: Taken together, the α-helical NTD of ClpB chaperones and the beta-stranded N-lobe of MtaLonA NTD comprise substrate-binding sites that play similar roles in specifically recognizing exposed hydrophobic stretches in unfolded or aggregated proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of the two systems.

claim: The binding events with damaged Ig2, scrambled lysozyme, and Sul20 peptide are mediated by two hydrophobic patches comprising L10, V14, I15, P22, V23, M85 (hpI) and M75, L77, P78, L82 (hpII).
source: By analyzing the NTD of MtaLonA interactions with damaged Ig2, the scrambled lysozyme, and Sul20 peptide, we conclude that these binding events are mediated by two hydrophobic patches, which comprise (1) L10, V14, I15, P22, V23, and M85 (termed hpI in the following); (2) M75, L77, P78, and L82 (termed hpII) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on NMR CSP mapping shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A double mutant NN206* (P22 and M85 replaced by Alanine) has a significant effect on the ability of MtaLonA NTD to bind damaged proteins.
source: Our results also demonstrate that a double mutant NN206* (P22 and M85 replaced by Alanine), resulted in decreased hydrophobicity of hpI, has a significant effect on the ability of MtaLonA NTD to bind damaged proteins, indicating that the hydrophobic patches can be essential for substrate recognition and discrimination.
evidence: This is supported by NMR binding studies with the mutant.

claim: The hydrophobic patches can be essential for substrate recognition and discrimination.
source: Our results also demonstrate that a double mutant NN206* (P22 and M85 replaced by Alanine), resulted in decreased hydrophobicity of hpI, has a significant effect on the ability of MtaLonA NTD to bind damaged proteins, indicating that the hydrophobic patches can be essential for substrate recognition and discrimination.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis studies.

claim: The N-terminal fragment from B. subtilis LonA was previously reported to adopt a domain-swapped dimer where the N-lobe of one monomer is positioned next to the C-lobe of the other monomer.
source: The N-terminal fragment from B. subtilis LonA was previously reported to adopt a domain-swapped dimer where the N-lobe of one monomer is positioned next to the C-lobe of the other monomer (Duman and Löwe, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Duman and Löwe, 2010.

claim: The structures of the N-terminal fragments from MtaLon, EcLon, and MacLon show that the N- and C-lobes are joined together via a short linker.
source: In contrast, the structures of the N-terminal fragments from MtaLon, EcLon, and MacLon show that the N- and C-lobes are joined together via a short linker (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The N-lobe of EcLon has almost the same pattern of exposed hydrophobic residues as that of MtaLon NTD.
source: Based on structural alignments (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), the N-lobe of EcLon has almost the same pattern of exposed hydrophobic residues as that of MtaLon NTD (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The NTD of MacLon shows merged hp I and II.
source: Interestingly, the NTD of MacLon shows merged hp I and II, while the hpI of BsLon NTD is a little distant from hpII (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The hpI of BsLon NTD is a little distant from hpII.
source: Interestingly, the NTD of MacLon shows merged hp I and II, while the hpI of BsLon NTD is a little distant from hpII (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: All three reported structures exhibit exposed hp I and II with slight variations in their shapes and sizes.
source: The structural comparison reveals that, similarly to MtaLon NTD, all three reported structures exhibit exposed hp I and II with slight variations in their shapes and sizes, suggesting that the conserved hydrophobic patches at the N-lobes may be potentially responsible for conferring substrate selectivity toward damaged proteins and degrons.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison of multiple LonA NTDs.

claim: The conserved hydrophobic patches at the N-lobes may be potentially responsible for conferring substrate selectivity toward damaged proteins and degrons.
source: The structural comparison reveals that, similarly to MtaLon NTD, all three reported structures exhibit exposed hp I and II with slight variations in their shapes and sizes, suggesting that the conserved hydrophobic patches at the N-lobes may be potentially responsible for conferring substrate selectivity toward damaged proteins and degrons.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural conservation.

claim: The C-terminal Sul20 has substantially low heteronuclear NOE values, reflecting this region undergoes rapid local motion and is solvent exposed in solution.
source: Here, our results show the C-terminal Sul20 has substantially low heteronuclear NOE values, reflecting this region undergoes rapid local motion and is solvent exposed in solution.
evidence: This is supported by NOE measurements.

claim: MtaLonA NTD can easily recognize and interact with the C-terminal aromatic and hydrophobic residues of Sul20.
source: Therefore, MtaLonA NTD can easily recognize and interact with the C-terminal aromatic and hydrophobic residues of Sul20.
evidence: This is inferred from the flexibility and exposure of Sul20.

claim: A pair of aromatic residues consisting of Y19 and H20 in Sul20 may play crucial roles in the hydrophobic interactions with residues P22 and M85 of MtaLonA NTD.
source: This finding indicates that a pair of aromatic residues consisting of Y19 and H20 in Sul20 may play crucial roles in the hydrophobic interactions with residues P22 and M85 of MtaLonA NTD, which is verified with a double-mutant NN206*.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis studies.

claim: The exposed substrate regions with aromatic or hydrophobic side chains are main determinants for their engagement with NN206.
source: The analysis of the interaction of NN206 or NN206* with Ig2D5-S20 or Ig2D5-S20-Y19A/H20A suggests that the exposed substrate regions with aromatic or hydrophobic side chains are main determinants for their engagement with NN206, which forms a binding site with similar hydrophobic residues.
evidence: This is inferred from the binding and mutagenesis studies.

claim: The primarily hydrophobic or aromatic interactions with NN206 do not lead to specific disorder-to-order transition of the substrate.
source: The primarily hydrophobic or aromatic interactions with NN206, however, do not lead to specific disorder-to-order transition of the substrate, forming for example an extended or helical structures in the bound state.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data showing Sul20 remains disordered upon binding.

claim: Specific backbone or side-chain interactions are not involved in substrate binding by NN206.
source: Perhaps, specific backbone or side-chain interactions are not involved in substrate binding by NN206.
evidence: This is speculated based on the lack of disorder-to-order transition.

claim: The N-lobe of NN206 engages non-specific interactions with non-contiguous patches of exposed hydrophobic residues of the substrates.
source: Rather, the N-lobe of NN206 engages non-specific interactions with non-contiguous patches of exposed hydrophobic residues of the substrates, thereby serving a role mainly to trap the substrates and keep them to the proximity of the AAA+ ring.
evidence: This is inferred from the binding characteristics observed.

claim: The N-lobe of NN206 serves a role mainly to trap the substrates and keep them to the proximity of the AAA+ ring.
source: Rather, the N-lobe of NN206 engages non-specific interactions with non-contiguous patches of exposed hydrophobic residues of the substrates, thereby serving a role mainly to trap the substrates and keep them to the proximity of the AAA+ ring.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation based on the binding data.

claim: By selectively binding to hydrophobic residues exposed in the thermally unfolded states of proteins, the NTDs prominently stabilize substrate's unfolded conformation.
source: Furthermore, by selectively binding to hydrophobic residues exposed in the thermally unfolded states of proteins, the NTDs prominently stabilize substrate's unfolded conformation.
evidence: This is supported by temperature cycling experiments.

claim: The NTD–substrate interactions involve the hydrophobic residues on both partners.
source: These results show that the NTD–substrate interactions involve the hydrophobic residues on both partners, suggesting aromatic and hydrophobic side chains, which are usually buried in the native proteins, are important for the NTD to enable MtaLonA to selectively capture and degrade proteins in a damaged unfolded state or with degron tags.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the binding and mutagenesis studies.

claim: Aromatic and hydrophobic side chains, which are usually buried in the native proteins, are important for the NTD to enable MtaLonA to selectively capture and degrade proteins in a damaged unfolded state or with degron tags.
source: These results show that the NTD–substrate interactions involve the hydrophobic residues on both partners, suggesting aromatic and hydrophobic side chains, which are usually buried in the native proteins, are important for the NTD to enable MtaLonA to selectively capture and degrade proteins in a damaged unfolded state or with degron tags.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on all the experimental data.

claim: Thermally damaged proteins and degrons induce chemical shift changes and broadened resonances located mainly in the two hydrophobic patches of N-terminal lobe.
source: Our results directly demonstrate that thermally damaged proteins and degrons induce chemical shift changes and broadened resonances located mainly in the two hydrophobic patches of N-terminal lobe, but we do not find evidence that the C-lobe of the NTD is involved in substrate interaction.
evidence: This is supported by NMR CSP mapping.

claim: There is no evidence that the C-lobe of the NTD is involved in substrate interaction with isolated NTD.
source: Our results directly demonstrate that thermally damaged proteins and degrons induce chemical shift changes and broadened resonances located mainly in the two hydrophobic patches of N-terminal lobe, but we do not find evidence that the C-lobe of the NTD is involved in substrate interaction.
evidence: This is based on NMR CSP mapping with isolated NTD.

claim: Upon titration of thermally unfolded Ig2 into full-length LonA*, affected residues were shown in both N- and C-lobes of MtaLonA* NTD at 55°C.
source: However, upon titration of thermally unfolded Ig2 into U-2H/15N-labelled full-length LonA*, affected residues were shown in both N- and C-lobes of MtaLonA* NTD at 55°C (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: The signals from the C-lobe of MtaLonA* NTD showed notable line broadening in the presence of thermally unfolded Ig2.
source: Compared 1H–15N TROSY-HSQC spectra of protonated NN206 and highly deuterated MtaLonA* in the presence of thermally unfolded protein Ig2, the signals from the C-lobe of MtaLonA* NTD showed notable line broadening, suggesting that other NTDs of LonA* hexamer may join to interact with substrates.
evidence: This is supported by NMR spectral comparison.

claim: Other NTDs of LonA* hexamer may join to interact with substrates.
source: Compared 1H–15N TROSY-HSQC spectra of protonated NN206 and highly deuterated MtaLonA* in the presence of thermally unfolded protein Ig2, the signals from the C-lobe of MtaLonA* NTD showed notable line broadening, suggesting that other NTDs of LonA* hexamer may join to interact with substrates.
evidence: This is inferred from the line broadening of C-lobe signals in full-length LonA.

claim: When one NTD of LonA hexamer binds to and tethers a substrate nearby, it would be easier for other NTDs to make further substrate contacts.
source: It is likely that when a substrate like Ig2 becomes damaged or partially unfolded one or more Lon binding sites are exposed. The multiple NTDs in the ~0.5 MDa hexameric assembly of LonA can work as team players and show the avidity effect on substrate binding. When one NTD of LonA hexamer binds to and tethers a substrate nearby, it would be easier for other NTDs to make further substrate contacts.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the NMR data with full-length LonA.

claim: The multiple NTDs in the ~0.5 MDa hexameric assembly of LonA can work as team players and show the avidity effect on substrate binding.
source: It is likely that when a substrate like Ig2 becomes damaged or partially unfolded one or more Lon binding sites are exposed. The multiple NTDs in the ~0.5 MDa hexameric assembly of LonA can work as team players and show the avidity effect on substrate binding.
